```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

This guide explains estimation and interpretation after the
[Get started](https://ksublee.github.io/emhawkes/articles/example.html) workflow.
See [Extended examples](https://ksublee.github.io/emhawkes/articles/extended_example.html)
for model specifications and [Computation](https://ksublee.github.io/emhawkes/articles/computation.html)
for engines, gradients and Jacobians.

## Working example

The following bivariate model supplies the data used below.

```{r working-example-1}
library(emhawkes)

h <- new("hspec",
  mu = c(0.2, 0.2),
  alpha = matrix(c(0.5, 0.9, 0.9, 0.5), 2, byrow = TRUE),
  beta = matrix(2.25, 2, 2)
)
set.seed(1107)
path <- hsim(h, size = 1000)
fit <- hfit(h, path$inter_arrival, path$type)
summary(fit)
```

## Parameter sharing and fixed entries {#parameter-settings}

By default, `reduced = TRUE` treats equal starting values **within each parameter matrix** as one parameter. This example estimates four parameters: one for `mu`, two for `alpha`, and one for `beta`. `hfit()` explains this rule once before optimization.

Use `reduced = FALSE` to estimate the ten matrix entries separately, even when their starting values are equal. Function components share parameters by name under either setting. A zero in a numeric matrix is also a starting value; use a component function to fix selected entries at zero.

The following examples show how starting values change the parameter map.

```{r parameter-example-data}
hspec2 <- h
res2 <- path
```


The sharing rule is applied separately to each matrix; equal values in `mu` and
`alpha` do not link those components. The startup message lists matrices with
shared entries. Use `suppressMessages(hfit(...))` to hide it.

For example, if `alpha[1,1]` and `alpha[1,2]` have different initial values, `hfit` estimates them separately.
If they have the same initial value, `hfit` treats them as a single parameter.

The previous example uses a symmetric Hawkes model: `alpha` is symmetric, and all entries of `beta` are equal.

```{r}
print(hspec2)
```

```{r, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(1107)
res2 <- hsim(hspec2, size = 1000)
```

In the first example, all entries of `alpha0` are set to 0.75.
This constrains `alpha11`, `alpha12`, `alpha21`, and `alpha22` to share one estimated value, even though their simulation values differ.
The same rule applies within `mu0` and `beta0`.

```{r, warning=FALSE}
mu0 <- matrix(c(0.15, 0.15), nrow = 2)
alpha0 <- matrix(c(0.75, 0.75, 0.75, 0.75), nrow = 2, byrow=TRUE)
beta0 <- matrix(c(2.6, 2.6, 2.6, 2.6), nrow = 2, byrow=TRUE)

hspec0 <- new("hspec", mu=mu0, alpha=alpha0, beta=beta0)
summary(hfit(hspec0, inter_arrival = res2$inter_arrival, type = res2$type))
```

This fit estimates one excitation parameter for both self-excitation and mutual excitation, whose simulation values are 0.5 and 0.9, respectively.

In the second example, `alpha0` has the same symmetry as the simulation model.
Its diagonal entries are equal, and its off-diagonal entries share a different value.
The model therefore has two excitation parameters to estimate.

```{r, warning=FALSE}
mu0 <- matrix(c(0.15, 0.15), nrow = 2)
alpha0 <- matrix(c(0.75, 0.751, 0.751, 0.75), nrow = 2, byrow=TRUE)
beta0 <- matrix(c(2.6, 2.6, 2.6, 2.6), nrow = 2, byrow=TRUE)

hspec0 <- new("hspec", mu=mu0, alpha=alpha0, beta=beta0)
summary(hfit(hspec0, inter_arrival = res2$inter_arrival, type = res2$type))
```

The third example allows `mu1` and `mu2` to differ, even though they are equal in the simulation model.

```{r, warning=FALSE}
mu0 <- matrix(c(0.15, 0.14), nrow = 2)
alpha0 <- matrix(c(0.75, 0.751, 0.751, 0.75), nrow = 2, byrow=TRUE)
beta0 <- matrix(c(2.6, 2.6, 2.6, 2.6), nrow = 2, byrow=TRUE)

hspec0 <- new("hspec", mu=mu0, alpha=alpha0, beta=beta0)
summary(hfit(hspec0, inter_arrival = res2$inter_arrival, type = res2$type))
```

Set `reduced = FALSE` to estimate each matrix entry separately, including entries with equal initial values.

```{r, warning=FALSE}
summary(hfit(hspec2, inter_arrival = res2$inter_arrival, type = res2$type, reduced=FALSE))
```

The same rules apply to higher-dimensional models.
For function components, the named entries in `param` define the estimated parameters.
Matching parameter names are shared across functions, even with `reduced = FALSE`.
Use different names for independent parameters with equal starting values.
Conflicting starting values for a shared name produce a warning, and the first value is used.
A zero in a numeric matrix is an estimated starting value; constants inside a component function remain fixed.


## Observed data and initial state

The first data row is the initial state. `inter_arrival`, `type`, and `mark` start with zero, followed by the observed events. `hsim(size)` includes this initial row. `N0` and `Nc0` specify initial counts and mark totals; `Nc0` must be named in `hfit()`.

The likelihood ends at the last supplied event. `N0` and `Nc0` accept a scalar
or one value per event type. Supplied `N` and `Nc` matrices must agree with the
event data and initial counts. Explicit `type_col_map` requires initial kernel
components for simulation and the built-in likelihood.


Event order is preserved when times coincide. Use the same initial counts and
`lambda_component0` for simulation and likelihood evaluation when comparing paths.
A scalar `lambda_component0` is expanded to all kernel components; a matrix must
match the kernel dimensions. For multi-kernel models, supply it explicitly.

Counting-process matrices supplied as `N` or `Nc` must agree with the event data and initial counts.
Each row contains the values after that event.
A baseline function called with index `n` uses row `n - 1` for the preceding state; an impact function uses row `n` for the current event.
Component functions can declare only the arguments they need, and use `...` to receive the remaining context.

Prepare observed event times measured from the observation start as follows:

```{r observed-input, eval=FALSE}
inter_arrival <- c(0, diff(c(0, event_times)))
type <- c(0, event_types)
mark <- c(0, event_marks)
```

Omit `type` for a univariate model and `mark` for unit marks.
The vectors must have the same length; event types range from 1 to the model dimension.

## Restoring and saving a fitted model

Use `fitted_hspec(fit)` to restore the estimated model and
`fit_initial_state(fit)` to retrieve the initial-state arguments:

```{r restored-model-1}
estimated <- fitted_hspec(fit)
initial <- fit_initial_state(fit)
inferred <- do.call(logLik, c(list(object = estimated,
  inter_arrival = path$inter_arrival, type = path$type, mark = path$mark,
  infer = TRUE), initial))
```

The result remains a `maxLik` object, so `coef()`, `summary()`, and `vcov()` keep
their existing behavior. The saved parameter map preserves shared parameters and
fixed constants in component functions. Simulation generators are retained, and
their named parameters are updated when they match estimated coefficient names.
Automatic initial intensity remains `NULL` and is recalculated for the restored
model. Initial counts are retained. A custom objective is not incorporated into
the restored model.

Save the fit with `saveRDS()` to retain this information between sessions.
Keep the observed data separately and supply them again for inference. The stored
optimization objective can retain data in its function environment.
The saved initial state describes the start of the observation window. Pass it
to `hsim()` to start a new path from the estimated model. Continuing after the
last observed event requires that event's state. Fits created without the new
metadata need to be refitted before using the reconstruction helpers.

Pass the restored specification and the saved initial-state arguments to
`hsim()` to generate a new path after checking convergence and model suitability.

```{r fitted-simulation, message=FALSE}
set.seed(1108)
simulated <- do.call(hsim, c(list(object = estimated, size = 100), initial))
head(simulated$arrival)
```

```{r save-fit, eval=FALSE}
saveRDS(fit, "hawkes-fit.rds")
saved_fit <- readRDS("hawkes-fit.rds")
estimated <- fitted_hspec(saved_fit)
initial <- fit_initial_state(saved_fit)
```

## Curvature and standard errors

By default, `hfit()` uses the final Hessian and standard errors from `maxLik`.
It does not run the additional stabilization checks. If numerical Hawkes
standard errors contain `NaN`, a short message suggests trying
`final_hessian = "stable"`. Request this option to check numerical Hawkes
curvature with scaled central differences and Richardson extrapolation.
With `auto` or `cpp`, stable curvature differentiates the built-in analytic score
when the model is supported and any required component Jacobians are supplied.
This also works with the default numerical optimizer gradient. Unsupported score
models, missing Jacobians, or failed score evaluations use likelihood differences;
`r` always uses likelihood differences. Inspect `curvature_source` and
`score_fallback_reason` in `fit_diagnostics(fit)` for the selected path.
This preserves the optimizer's
coefficients and log-likelihood. `summary()` and `vcov()` then use the checked
covariance; free-parameter standard errors are `NA` when stable inversion is
unavailable. Inspect `fit_diagnostics(fit)` for the requested checks.
Supplied Hessians, disabled final curvature, BHHH, custom objectives, and residual
models retain their calculation choices.

For unconstrained BFGS, CG, Nelder-Mead, and SANN fits without supplied `hess`
or `finalHessian`, stable curvature omits maxLik's separate final Hessian.
Inspect `fit_diagnostics(fit)$computation$hessian$maxLik_skipped`; the omitted
matrix is not stored in `original_hessian`. Use `finalHessian = TRUE` to retain
that extra calculation. The default `final_hessian = "maxLik"` is unchanged.

A stable Hessian does not guarantee reliable Wald intervals. Nearby kernel decay
rates, weak excitation, boundaries, short samples, and nonsmooth callbacks can
still make inference unreliable. The [Hawkes standard-error report](https://github.com/ksublee/emhawkes/blob/main/tools/hawkes-standard-errors.md)
compares unchanged estimates and corrected standard errors, and discusses profile
likelihood and bootstrap. The [earlier diagnostic report](https://github.com/ksublee/emhawkes/blob/main/tools/fit-diagnostics.md)
records the original Hawkes and FRPP issues.

Check convergence, score, and multiple starting values before interpreting intervals.

For otherwise identical kernels driven by the same events, equal decay rates can
leave only the combined amplitude identifiable. Small excitation alone does not
require missing standard errors: known initial excitation can still carry decay
information. See the [Hawkes curvature stress checks](https://github.com/ksublee/emhawkes/blob/main/tools/stable-stress-results.md).

For checked fits, an unsuccessful optimizer triggers a warning even when stable
curvature is unavailable. Inspect `optimizer_success`, `optimizer_code` and
`warnings` in `fit_diagnostics(fit)` alongside its curvature `status` and `reason`.

```{r fit-curvature-diagnostics}
fit_checked <- hfit(h, path$inter_arrival, path$type, final_hessian = "stable")
fit_diagnostics(fit_checked)[c("status", "scaled_condition", "newton_decrement")]
```

The calculation record is explained in
[Computation](https://ksublee.github.io/emhawkes/articles/computation.html#recorded-calculation-methods).

## Residual diagnostics {#residual-process}

`logLik(h, ..., infer = TRUE)` returns a list with the likelihood, intensity
paths, and residual vectors. Use it in place of the deprecated `infer_lambda()`
and `residual_process()` helpers. Simulation returns an `hreal` object.


Set `infer = TRUE` in `logLik` to obtain the log-likelihood, intensity paths, and residual processes.
These are computed using the parameters in the supplied `hspec` object.
For a univariate model, `res_process1` contains the residual inter-arrival times.

```{r, warning=FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.height=4.5, fig.width=4.5}
hrp <- new("hspec", mu = 0.3, alpha = 1.2, beta = 1.5)
res_rp <- hsim(hrp, size = 1000)

# inferred result
infered_res <- logLik(hrp, res_rp$inter_arrival, infer = TRUE)

## QQ-plot
p <- ppoints(100)
q <- quantile(infered_res$res_process1, p = p)
plot(qexp(p), q, xlab="Theoretical Quantiles",ylab="Sample Quantiles")
qqline(q, distribution=qexp,col="blue", lty=2)
```

For observed data, estimate the parameters before computing the residual processes.

```{r, message=FALSE, fig.height=4.5, fig.width=4.5}

# estimation
mle_rp <- hfit(new("hspec", mu = 0.2, alpha = 1, beta = 2),
               res_rp$inter_arrival)

# Restore the estimated model and the initial-state arguments.
he <- fitted_hspec(mle_rp)
initial_rp <- fit_initial_state(mle_rp)

# infer intensity
infered_res <- do.call(logLik, c(list(object = he,
  inter_arrival = res_rp$inter_arrival, type = res_rp$type, infer = TRUE), initial_rp))

rpe <- infered_res$res_process1

p <- ppoints(100)
q <- quantile(rpe, p=p)
plot(qexp(p), q, xlab="Theoretical Quantiles",ylab="Sample Quantiles")
qqline(q, distribution=qexp,col="blue", lty=2)
```

For an $n$-dimensional model, `logLik` returns one residual process for each event type.
In the following bivariate example, these are `infer_res2$res_process1` and `infer_res2$res_process2`.

```{r, message=FALSE, fig.height=4.5, fig.width=4.5}
hrp2 <- new("hspec", mu = rep(0.3, 2),
           alpha = matrix(c(1.2, 1.5, 1.5, 1.2), nrow=2),
           beta = matrix(rep(3, 4), nrow=2))
res_hrp2 <- hsim(hrp2, size = 2000)

infer_res2 <- logLik(hrp2, res_hrp2$inter_arrival, res_hrp2$type, infer = TRUE)

p <- ppoints(100)
q <- quantile(c(infer_res2$res_process1, infer_res2$res_process2), p=p)
plot(qexp(p), q, xlab="Theoretical Quantiles",ylab="Sample Quantiles")
qqline(q, distribution=qexp,col="blue", lty=2)
```

```{r, message = FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.height=4, fig.width=6}
# Plot the pooled residuals for both event types.

hist(
  c(infer_res2$res_process1, infer_res2$res_process2),
  breaks = 50,
  probability = TRUE,
  main = "Histogram of Inferred Residual Process",
  xlab = "Residual Value",
  ylab = "Density"
)

x <- seq(0, 8, 0.1)

lines(
  x,
  dexp(x),
  col = 'red',
  lwd = 2
)

legend("topright", legend = "Theoretical PDF", col = "red", lwd = 2)

```


Residual checks assess model adequacy; they do not replace convergence or curvature checks.
See the [flexible residual examples](https://ksublee.github.io/emhawkes/articles/extended_example.html#point-processes-with-flexible-residuals)
for models with a non-exponential residual law.
